title: Ang 432–434: the Patti
hookLine: Guru Nanak's poem of the letters
tomorrow: what does a wedding song have to do with God?

lines: DID A BOY REALLY WRITE IT?
cards: Ask a kid what they learned at school today, and the answer is often: nothing. A story Sikhs tell goes the other way.

When young Nanak was sent to learn his letters, he had something to teach back: for each letter, a line about the One, written on the wooden slate. That poem sits on ang 432. It's called the Patti, the writing board.
But did a boy really write it?

teach.b: The Patti walks through the Gurmukhi letters one by one. It opens, in paraphrase: sassa, the One who made the world is the one master of all. Between the letters comes a refrain: why forget, foolish mind?

teach.h: EDUCATED: ABLE TO GIVE AN ACCOUNT.
teach.b: When you give your account, brother, then you'll be counted educated. Real learning, it says, is whether you can answer for your life. Now the debate, and both sides are people who love this hymn.
One view comes from the Janamsakhis, the old life stories of Guru Nanak: the young Guru recited it to his teacher, and the teacher bowed.

teach.h: THE STORY: A BOY TEACHES BACK.
teach.b: For some families that story is the doorway into the hymn, and it carries something true: wisdom can come from the youngest person in the room.
The other view, held by some scholars, reads the Patti as written later in life, because it's so deep and so finished; on that reading, the Janamsakhi wraps a grown teaching in a childhood scene.
Both agree it is Guru Nanak's, and both point to the refrain.
The story asks who can teach. The scholars ask when. The hymn asks you: what's your account?

how: The Patti is read in order in Raag Asa and sung as kirtan; the Janamsakhi story of the young Guru Nanak and his teacher is told in Sikh homes and Sikh schools.

o: it carries a true point: wisdom can come from the youngest in the room.

practice: Open ang 432 if you can and find the first letter, sassa, ਸ. Trace it with a finger, or write it on paper, slowly, a few times.
Then rest, and let the refrain sit beside you: when you give your account, then you're counted educated.
